content: The Consolidated Guidelines on Person-Centred Viral Hepatitis Strategic Information outlines a comprehensive approach to using data to support the scaling up of hepatitis prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services at the country level. The guidelines emphasize the importance of person-centred monitoring and evaluation systems, focusing on core indicators that address prevention, diagnosis, and treatment interventions for hepatitis B and C. The publication is available in both electronic and print formats, with ISBNs 978-92-4-009131-3 and 978-92-4-009132-0, respectively. It is published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2024. Under the terms of the Creative Commons license, the content can be copied, redistributed, and adapted for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is not permitted, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, a disclaimer must be included, stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The guidelines provide a structured framework for monitoring and evaluation, organizing 10 core indicators along the results chain, from inputs to outputs, outcomes, and impact. These indicators aim to identify programmatic gaps and improve the focus of hepatitis programs. Key indicators include the prevalence of chronic hepatitis B and C, the existence of costed national strategic plans for hepatitis elimination, vaccination coverage, testing and diagnosis rates, treatment coverage, and outcomes such as cure rates and mortality reduction. The document also highlights the importance of strengthening country surveillance systems. This includes validating existing data, identifying gaps, and using data for planning and scaling up services. Countries are encouraged to implement prevalence surveys, create person-centred treatment databases, and use drug consumption data to triangulate treatment data and identify gaps. The guidelines stress the integration of hepatitis data into routine health management information systems to ensure interoperability and routine use. They also emphasize the need for enhanced analysis of outcomes to improve the estimation of hepatitis-related sequelae and to inform programmatic decisions. The publication acknowledges the contributions of various individuals and organizations, including members of the Technical Working Group and WHO staff, who reviewed drafts and provided valuable input. Funding for the development of these guidelines was provided by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The glossary of terms included in the document defines key concepts such as acute and chronic viral hepatitis, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) as a marker of liver inflammation, and various serological markers for hepatitis B and C. It also explains the importance of strategic information, monitoring, and evaluation systems in improving programmatic outcomes. The guidelines aim to strengthen person-centred health services by focusing on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment interventions. They provide a stepwise approach to improving country-level data systems, ensuring that available data is used effectively to scale up hepatitis prevention and treatment services.
